kurals.tamil:
பாலொடு தேன்கலந் தற்றே பணிமொழி
வாலெயிறு ஊறிய நீர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Paalodu thaenkalandh thatrae panimozhi
vaaleyiru ooriya neer.
kurals.meaning: The moisture on the white teeth of this softly spoken girl is like milk and honey mixed together.
kurals.elementary: Think of the sweetest drink you can imagine, warm milk with a spoon of honey stirred in. The poet says that being close to the person he loves feels that sweet. It is his way of saying that love makes everything about the beloved seem delightful.
kurals.university: Chapter 113 belongs to the kalaviyal (the section on secret, premarital love) and opens with the hero speaking after union, declaring the special excellence (sirappu) of the love itself rather than of the beloved's looks, which was the topic of ch. 112. Pani-mozhi (பணிமொழி, 'gentle, deferential speech') names the heroine by her soft voice, and vaal-eyiru (வாலெயிறு, 'white teeth') is a stock feature of the akam heroine; ooriya neer ('the water that wells up') is a decorous image for the sweetness of a kiss. Milk-and-honey (paalodu thaen) is the classical Tamil figure for perfect sweetness; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss the line this way, Pope renders 'The dew on her white teeth, whose voice is soft and low, / Is as when milk and honey mingled flow', and the commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar reads the chapter's first five couplets as the hero's words. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In an Atharvaveda love charm the speaker declares that honey is on the tip and at the root of his tongue, asking that his speech and presence become as sweet as honey to the one he loves.
hinduism.explanation: The hymn uses honey (madhu) as the measure of sweetness that love should carry between two people.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it reaches for honey on the tongue to express the sweetness of lovers' closeness.
hinduism.source: Atharvaveda 1.34 (charm with licorice to secure a woman's love; cf. tr. Maurice Bloomfield, SBE 42) (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of a well-known hymn, not checked word for word this session; the honey-on-the-tongue image matches, but it is a spell, not a lover's praise.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs opens with the beloved longing for a kiss and ranking love above the best drink she knows.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise ranks the sweetness of the beloved's mouth above the finest drink, milk mixed with honey.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); same move of comparing a kiss to a delicious drink, with wine instead of milk and honey.

islam.quote_or_event: “rivers of milk the taste of which never changes, rivers of wine delicious to those who drink, and rivers of purified honey”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes Paradise with rivers of unspoiled milk and purified honey as images of perfect, lasting delight.
islam.tie_back: Milk and honey stand for supreme sweetness in both texts, though the Qur'an applies it to Paradise, not to a lover.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; the milk-and-honey pairing matches closely, but the subject is reward in the hereafter, not romantic love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thy lips, O my bride, drop honey— Honey and milk are under thy tongue”
judaism.explanation: The lover of the Song of Songs says that honey and milk lie under his bride's tongue.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own image: the beloved's mouth holds milk and honey.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a near one-to-one match of image and sentiment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the opening suttas of the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha says he knows of no other taste that so overpowers a man's mind as the taste of a woman, and likewise for a woman and the taste of a man.
buddhism.explanation: The point is a warning: the sweetness lovers find in each other is the strongest of sensual bonds.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural celebrates exactly this overpowering sweetness; Buddhism names it in order to loosen its grip.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; it recognises the same sweetness but treats it as a fetter, the opposite evaluation.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain sermon on carelessness compares sensual pleasure to a fruit that tastes sweet but proves poisonous.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural savours a sweetness like milk and honey, the Jain text warns that such sweetness is the bait of karmic bondage.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares the image of sweet taste but reverses the Kural's judgment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Homer introduces old Nestor, the clear-voiced speaker of Pylos, as a man from whose tongue speech flowed sweeter than honey.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek epic, like Tamil poetry, uses honey as the measure of sweet and gentle speech.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's heroine is pani-mozhi, 'soft of speech', and her mouth is likened to honey in the same way.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 1.247-249 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; the honey-sweet speech image fits, but Nestor is an elder counsellor, not a beloved.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that self-indulgence and temperance concern the pleasures of touch and taste, the pleasures humans share with other animals, and that the self-indulgent delight above all in touch.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle these are the pleasures most in need of moderation because they are the most immediate.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural lingers over exactly such a pleasure of taste and touch, treating it as the high point of love rather than as a test of temperance.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; a next-best match that discusses the same kind of pleasure from a moral distance.

kurals.tamil:
உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை என்னமற் றன்ன
மடந்தையொடு எம்மிடை நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Udambodu uyiridai ennamat ranna
madandhaiyodu emmidai natpu.
kurals.meaning: Whatever the bond is between body and life, such is the bond between this young woman and me.
kurals.elementary: Your body and the life inside it always go together; you can't send one to school and leave the other at home. The poet says he and the person he loves belong together in that same way.
kurals.university: The hero now states the inseparability of the lovers through the classic Indian pairing of udambu (உடம்பு, body) and uyir (உயிர், life or soul). The word chosen for the relationship is natpu (நட்பு, 'friendship, intimacy'), the same term that heads the Porutpaal chapters on friendship (ch. 79 onward), so the love is presented as a perfect friendship. Madandhai (மடந்தை) denotes a young woman, conventionally of marriageable age. Modern commentators agree on the sense: Mu. Varadarasanar ('as the ties between body and life'), Solomon Pappaiah ('the relation between body and life'), Kalaignar ('life and body never live apart; such is our relationship'); Pope translates 'Between this maid and me the friendship kind / Is as the bonds that soul and body bind.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Rigvedic wedding hymn the couple pray that the gods and the waters join their two hearts together into one.
hinduism.explanation: The verse is still recited at Hindu weddings as the moment the two lives are declared united.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes the bond of lovers as a union so close that two become one.
hinduism.source: Rigveda 10.85.47 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Ralph T.H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a strong thematic fit, though it is a marriage blessing rather than the Kural's body-and-life image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. He that loveth his wife loveth himself.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells husbands that a wife is as much a part of a man as his own body.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes the beloved as inseparable from the lover as life is from the body.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); strong fit on the body image, though Paul's frame is marital duty rather than the Kural's lyric declaration.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes husband and wife as garments for each other: closest to the body, protecting and covering one another.
islam.tie_back: Both texts pick the thing nearest the self, clothing or the body itself, to show how close the lovers are.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; close in spirit, with the garment as a less absolute image than body and life.

judaism.quote_or_event: “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh … and they shall be one flesh.”
judaism.explanation: On first seeing the woman, Adam recognises her as part of his own body, and the Torah adds that husband and wife become one flesh.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover too finds the beloved to be part of his very being.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria with an ellipsis joining verses 23 and 24; strong match on the lovers sharing one body.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If both husband & wife want to see one another not only in the present life but also in the life to come, they should be in tune [with each other] in conviction, in tune in virtue, in tune in generosity, and in tune in discernment.”
buddhism.explanation: When the devoted couple Nakula's father and mother ask to be together in future lives, the Buddha tells them how.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's bond as close as body and life finds its Buddhist counterpart in a couple joined across lives by shared virtue.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight; a strong fit on inseparable married love, grounded in virtue rather than passion.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Sutrakritanga refutes the materialists who hold that the soul is the same as the body, insisting that soul and body are distinct, like a sword that can be drawn from its scabbard.
jainism.explanation: For Jainism the soul (jiva) is only temporarily bound to a body by karma, and liberation means separating them for good.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's ideal of a bond like body and life is, for a Jain, the very bond to be loosened, so the parallel is one of sharp contrast.
jainism.source: Sutrakritanga 2.1 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the sword-and-scabbard argument, not checked word for word this session; it addresses the same body-and-soul image but with the opposite valuation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “human nature was originally one and we were a whole, and the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aristophanes' myth, humans were once double beings that Zeus split in two, and love is each half seeking its other half.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's lovers belong together as body and life do; Aristophanes says lovers are literally two halves of one being.
greek_mythology.source: Plato, Symposium 192e-193a, speech of Aristophanes (tr. Benjamin Jowett)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive; a near one-to-one match of the idea of lovers as one being.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Asked what a friend is, Aristotle is reported to have answered: a single soul dwelling in two bodies.
philosophy.explanation: The saying sums up Aristotle's view that perfect friendship makes two people share one life.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural even calls the love natpu, friendship, and makes it as close as soul and body.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 5.20 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested saying, not checked word for word this session; it is reported anecdote rather than Aristotle's own writing.

kurals.tamil:
கருமணியிற் பாவாய்நீ போதாயாம் வீழும்
திருநுதற்கு இல்லை இடம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Karumaniyir paavaainee poadhaayaam veezhum
thirunudharku illai idam.
kurals.meaning: O little image in the pupil of my eye, go away; there is no room there for the fair-browed one I love.
kurals.elementary: When you look closely into someone's eye you can see a tiny picture of yourself in it. The poet tells that tiny picture to move out, because he wants his eye to hold only the person he loves.
kurals.university: The conceit rests on paavai (பாவை, 'doll, image'), the tiny reflected figure visible in the karumani (கருமணி, the dark pupil); the lover orders it to leave (poadhaai) because there is no idam (இடம், 'room') for thiru-nudhal (திருநுதல், 'she of the lovely brow'), a standard epithet for the heroine. The idea is that he wants to hold her image permanently in his sight. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree; Pope: 'For her with beauteous brow, the maid I love, there place is none; / To give her image room, O pupil of mine eye, begone!' Pulavar Kesikan's gloss adds 'there is no other place for her to stay', heightening the hyperbole. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Chandogya Upanishad, Prajapati first teaches that the person seen in the eye is the Self, a lesson Indra later finds incomplete.
hinduism.explanation: The figure reflected in the pupil was an old Indian puzzle, and the Upanishad uses it as a first step toward knowing the true Self.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural plays with the same figure in the eye but wants to replace it with the beloved, turning a metaphysical image into a lover's one.
hinduism.source: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7.4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 1)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; it shares the image of the figure in the pupil but has a philosophical purpose, not a romantic one.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist asks God to guard him as carefully as one guards the pupil of the eye.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat the pupil as the most cherished place, the place where the dearest one is kept.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); the Hebrew idiom ('little man of the eye') is the same pupil image, but the context is prayer, not love.

islam.quote_or_event: “Our Lord, grant us from among our wives and offspring comfort to our eyes”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises those who pray that their spouses and children be qurrat a'yun, a delight or coolness to their eyes.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's lover wants his eyes filled with his beloved; the Qur'an calls a spouse the comfort of one's eyes.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; a genuine eye-and-beloved idiom, though as a prayer within marriage rather than a lover's conceit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When our love was strong, we could have slept on a bed that was the width of a sword. Now that our love is not strong, a bed of sixty cubits is not sufficient for us.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud records a popular saying about marriage: love makes the smallest space enough, and its lack makes any space too small.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover finds no room in his eye except for her; the Talmudic saying likewise measures love by how much space it needs.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 7a (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria (translator's bold markup removed); a lively parallel on love and space, though not about the eye.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Therigatha a man becomes infatuated with the nun Subha's eyes; she answers that the eye is only a ball of tissue and fluid and, to cure his obsession, plucks one out and gives it to him.
buddhism.explanation: The story uses the eye, the seat of attraction, to teach how infatuation fixes on a part of the body.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover fills his eye with his beloved; Subha's story treats such fixation as the illusion to be cut through.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a next-best match built on the eye image but pointing in the opposite direction.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of 'colours,' will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain sermon warns that the eye, captured by what it loves to see, leads the soul into ruin.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's lover wants his eye wholly taken up by the beloved's form; the Jain text calls that capture the moth's error.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; matches the theme of the eye held by a loved form but condemns it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Narcissus falls in love with the image he sees in a pool and cannot bear to leave it.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth turns on an image seen with the eyes that captures the viewer completely.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's lover banishes the image of himself from his pupil to make room for his beloved, exactly the reverse of Narcissus's fixation on himself.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; the image-in-the-eye theme matches, with self-love as the instructive contrast.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates points out that when a person looks into another's eye, his face is reflected in the pupil as in a mirror, which the Greeks call the 'kore', the girl or doll.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses this to argue that the soul comes to know itself by looking into another soul.
philosophy.tie_back: The Greek kore and the Tamil paavai are the same 'little doll' in the eye that the Kural's lover tells to leave.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a striking parallel of the doll-in-the-pupil image, used for self-knowledge rather than love.

kurals.tamil:
வாழ்தல் உயிர்க்கன்னள் ஆயிழை சாதல்
அதற்கன்னள் நீங்கும் இடத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaazhdhal uyirkkannal aayizhai saadhal
adharkannal neengum idaththu.
kurals.meaning: My finely jewelled love is like life to my soul when she is with me, and like death to it when she leaves.
kurals.elementary: When your best friend is with you the whole day feels bright, and when they go home it can feel empty and dark. The poet says the person he loves feels like life itself when near, and leaving feels like losing life.
kurals.university: The couplet balances vaazhdhal (வாழ்தல், living) against saadhal (சாதல், dying), with annal (அன்னள், 'she is like') repeated in each half and neengum idaththu ('at the time she departs') as the hinge. Aayizhai (ஆயிழை) is an epithet, 'she of chosen jewels'; Kalaignar extends it to 'she who wears chosen virtues as her ornaments'. Mu. Varadarasanar: 'when she joins me she is like life to my soul, when she parts she is like death to it'; Solomon Pappaiah reads the first half as 'like the body to the soul', a slightly different construal of the same syntax. Pope: 'Life is she to my very soul when she draws nigh; / Dissevered from the maid with jewels rare, I die!' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama tries to leave her behind for his forest exile, Sita answers that being with him is heaven and being without him is hell, and insists on going with him.
hinduism.explanation: In Valmiki's Ramayana Sita treats separation from her husband as worse than any hardship of the forest.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, she makes the beloved's presence life and his absence a kind of death.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda, Sita's plea to accompany Rama (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode, verse number not given because it varies between editions; a strong thematic fit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that his whole life is bound up with Christ, so that even death is welcome because it brings him closer.
christianity.tie_back: As the Kural's beloved is life to the lover, Christ is life itself to Paul, though Paul reverses the Kural's fear of death.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); the 'my life is the beloved' structure matches, but the love is devotional and the view of death opposite.

islam.quote_or_event: “He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents spouses as a source of rest and of a God-given affection between two people.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's beloved is the life of the lover's soul; the Qur'an speaks of a spouse as the one in whom the soul finds rest.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; a next-best match on spouses sustaining each other, with no life-and-death contrast.

judaism.explanation: After Honi awakes from seventy years of sleep and finds no one who recognises him, he prays for death, and Rava cites this folk saying.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover feels that losing his companion is like dying; the Talmud's saying says the same of losing all companionship.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; it matches the life-or-death weight given to companionship, but concerns friendship and community, not a lover.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the pain of parting comes from holding someone dear in the first place.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover feels parting as death; the Buddha recognises the same pain and points to non-attachment as the way out.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight; it describes the same experience of separation but draws the opposite lesson.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra names, as one form of 'sorrowful' (arta) meditation, the anguished brooding over separation from what one holds dear and the longing to be reunited with it.
jainism.explanation: Jainism classes this grief among the unwholesome states of mind that bind fresh karma to the soul.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's 'like death when she leaves' is exactly the state of mind the Jain text diagnoses as a karmic danger.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.30-34, on arta-dhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. Nathmal Tatia)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word and sutra numbering approximate; a precise doctrinal match to the experience, with the opposite evaluation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Eurydice dies, Orpheus descends to the underworld to bring her back; when he loses her a second time he grieves until his own death and refuses all other love.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes the loss of the beloved the end of the lover's life in all but name.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's lover says the beloved's departure is death to him; Orpheus lives that out.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely told myth; a strong fit on the beloved as life itself, though here the separation is literal death.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Love will make men dare to die for their beloved-love alone; andwomen as well as men. Of this, Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, is a monument to all Hellas; for she was willing to lay down her life on behalf of her husband”
philosophy.explanation: In Plato's Symposium, Phaedrus praises love as the force that makes lovers value each other above their own lives.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's beloved is the lover's life; Phaedrus's example shows a lover giving up her life for the beloved.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 179b, speech of Phaedrus (tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (spacing errors as printed there); love bound up with life and death, from the angle of self-sacrifice.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளுவன் மன்யான் மறப்பின் மறப்பறியேன்
ஒள்ளமர்க் கண்ணாள் குணம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ulluvan manyaan marappin marappariyaen
ollamark kannaal gunam.
kurals.meaning: If I ever forgot the qualities of the girl with bright, battling eyes, I could remember them; but I never forget them at all.
kurals.elementary: You only need to remember something if you have forgotten it. The poet says he never needs to remember the girl he loves, because she is never out of his mind for a moment.
kurals.university: The paradox turns on ulluvan (உள்ளுவன், 'I would recall') against marappu ariyaen (மறப்பறியேன், 'I do not know forgetting'): recollection presupposes forgetting, and since he never forgets her, he never has to 'remember' her. The particle man (மன்) marks the conditional as unrealised. Ol-amar-kannaal (ஒள்ளமர்க் கண்ணாள்) is read two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Pope take amar as 'battle', hence 'bright, warring eyes' (Pope: 'whose eyes gleam like the warrior's dart'), while Pulavar Kesikan reads ollivaai amarndha, 'bright and calmly set'. Pope's note, following the commentators, says the hero speaks to the heroine's maid (tozhi), who had asked whether he still remembered her. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Under the sage Durvasa's curse, King Dushyanta forgets Shakuntala entirely, until he sees the ring he gave her and his memory and love flood back.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa's drama turns on forgetting and remembering a beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's lover insists he can never forget; Kalidasa shows the anguish when a lover does forget and must remember again.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Acts IV-VI (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the play's plot; same theme of remembering and forgetting the beloved, approached through its opposite.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.”
christianity.explanation: God assures his people that his love is more unforgetting than even a mother's.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts define deepest love as the impossibility of forgetting the one loved.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a close match on the 'I cannot forget you' declaration, in a divine rather than romantic setting.

islam.quote_or_event: “I did not feel jealous of any of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) as much as I did of Khadija though I did not see her, but the Prophet (ﷺ) used to mention her very often”
islam.explanation: Aisha recalls that years after Khadija's death the Prophet kept speaking of her and honouring her friends.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's lover, the Prophet never forgot his beloved's qualities; she was always on his lips.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a strong fit on undying remembrance of a beloved wife.

judaism.quote_or_event: The exiles by the rivers of Babylon swear that if they ever forget Jerusalem, their right hand should lose its skill and their tongue cleave to the roof of the mouth.
judaism.explanation: The psalm makes forgetting the beloved city unthinkable, something they would rather be maimed than do.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover too declares forgetting impossible; the psalm's beloved is a city instead of a person.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified word for word this session; a good fit on unforgetting love, but for Zion, not a beloved woman.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The aged brahmin Pingiya tells his teacher that he is never apart from the Buddha even for a moment: he sees him with his mind as with his eye, day and night, and spends the nights paying him homage.
buddhism.explanation: His devotion is so constant that the Buddha is always present in his recollection.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover never has to remember his beloved because he never forgets; Pingiya describes the same unbroken recollection, directed to his teacher.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 5.18, Pingiya's verses at the close of the Parayana Vagga (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the online translations could not be loaded this session to verify wording, but the episode is well attested; devotional rather than romantic.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Sramana, engaged in penance, should not allow himself to watch the shape, beauty, coquetry, laughter, prattle, gestures, and glances of women, nor retain a recollection of them in his mind.”
jainism.explanation: Jain monastic discipline forbids even keeping the memory of a woman's charms.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's lover cannot stop recalling the qualities of his beloved; the Jain ascetic is told to let precisely such recollection go.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified in 'Sramana'); a direct counterpoint about remembering a beloved's charms, addressed to monks.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Kept for years on Calypso's island and offered immortality, Odysseus still sits on the shore longing for Penelope and home, and tells the goddess that he wants to go back to her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus's longing for his wife does not fade over long separation or in the face of a goddess's love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's lover, Odysseus cannot forget the qualities of the one he loves.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene; strong fit on unforgetting love despite separation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Montaigne writes that after the death of his friend Étienne de La Boétie he had grown so used to being one of two that he now felt only half himself, and that he had never stopped missing him.
philosophy.explanation: The essay on friendship describes a union of two souls so complete that the friend's absence is felt constantly.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover never forgets his beloved; Montaigne describes a friend who is never out of his mind years after his death.
philosophy.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays I.28, 'Of Friendship' (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a close parallel of constant remembrance, though about friendship rather than romantic love.

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார் இமைப்பின் பருகுவரா
நுண்ணியர்எம் காத லவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannullin poakaar imaippin paruguvaraa
nunniyarem kaadha lavar.
kurals.meaning: My lover never leaves my eyes, and even when I blink he is not hurt, so subtle and fine is he.
kurals.elementary: Imagine keeping a picture of someone you love in your mind so clearly that it stays even when you blink. Blinking can't hurt that picture because it is not made of anything solid. The girl in this poem says her love lives in her eyes like that.
kurals.university: With this couplet the voice passes to the heroine (talaivi), who answers her companion's worry that the hero is far away: he is always in her eyes. Kannullin poagaar (கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார், 'he does not leave from within my eyes') is followed by imaippin paruguvaraa (இமைப்பின் பருகுவரா, 'he does not suffer if I blink'), and nunniyar (நுண்ணியர், 'subtle, fine') explains why: he is too fine to be crushed by the eyelids. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pulavar Kesikan and Kalaignar all read paruguvaraa as 'will not be pained'; Solomon Pappaiah adds that 'others cannot perceive his subtle nature'. Pope takes it differently, 'I wink them not, lest I should pain him where he lies', which anticipates the not-blinking motif of 1129. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In a well-known bhajan, Mirabai asks Krishna, the son of Nanda, to come and dwell in her eyes.
hinduism.explanation: The bhakti poet speaks of her divine beloved as living within her sight at every moment.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says her lover never leaves her eyes; Mira makes the same request of Krishna.
hinduism.source: Mirabai, bhajan 'Baso more nainan mein Nandalal' (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a popular bhajan traditionally attributed to Mirabai; attribution and text vary between collections, and no English wording was verified this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go”
christianity.explanation: The woman in the Song of Songs finds her beloved after searching for him through the night and refuses to let him leave.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's heroine, she keeps her beloved close and will not let him go.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); shares the will to hold the beloved fast, though physically rather than in the eyes.

islam.quote_or_event: “To worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you cannot achieve this state of devotion then you must consider that He is looking at you.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet defines ihsan, the highest level of faith, as living as if the unseen Beloved were before one's eyes.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's heroine keeps her absent lover always before her eyes; ihsan asks the believer to keep God there.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; it matches the idea of an unseen presence held in sight, in a devotional rather than romantic context.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have set the LORD always before me; Surely He is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist keeps God continually before his eyes; the verse is often displayed in synagogues as a shiviti.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine keeps her beloved always within her eyes; the psalmist does the same with God.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; same habit of keeping the beloved one always in view, directed to God.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada traces anxiety for others to the affection we feel for them.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine worries that even her blinking might hurt her beloved; the Buddha would see that tender fear as born of endearment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight; a next-best match that diagnoses the heroine's anxious tenderness rather than sharing her image.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain philosophy classes the soul, like space and the principles of motion and rest, among the formless (arupa) substances; only matter has form, so the soul itself cannot be struck or crushed.
jainism.explanation: Because the soul has no material form, physical contact cannot injure it, even though the body it inhabits can be hurt.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine says her lover is too subtle to be harmed by her eyelids, which a Jain would say is literally true of the soul.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.4-5 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Nathmal Tatia)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word and sutra numbering approximate; a next-best doctrinal parallel to 'subtle', with no romantic content.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that from the eyes of the three Graces, as they glanced, flowed love that loosens the limbs, and that their glance from beneath their brows was beautiful.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth love itself is thought to pass through and dwell in the eyes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's heroine keeps her lover in her eyes; Hesiod makes the eyes the very fountain of love.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Theogony 907-911 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hugh G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a next-best match linking love and the eyes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius argues that the mind and soul are made of extremely small, smooth, round particles, so fine that when they leave the body at death its shape and weight seem unchanged.
philosophy.explanation: The Epicurean poet explains the subtlety of the soul by the fineness of its matter.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover is nunniyar, so subtle that blinking cannot hurt him; Lucretius gives a physical account of such subtlety.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; it matches the notion of extreme fineness only, with no romantic content.

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணுள்ளார் காத லவராகக் கண்ணும்
எழுதேம் கரப்பாக்கு அறிந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannullaar kaadha lavaraagak kannum
ezhudhaem karappaakku arindhu.
kurals.meaning: Because my lover lives in my eyes, I do not even line them with kohl, knowing it would hide him.
kurals.elementary: If you were keeping a tiny friend inside a glass jar, you wouldn't paint the jar, because then you couldn't see them. The girl in this poem doesn't put on eye makeup because she imagines her love is inside her eyes and the makeup would cover him.
kurals.university: The heroine continues the eye conceit: since her lover dwells in her eyes (kannullaar), she will not even 'write' her eyes (kannum ezhudhaem), ezhudhu (எழுது) being the Tamil verb for applying mai (மை, kohl or collyrium), for fear of karappu (கரப்பு, concealment) of him. Applying kohl was a basic daily adornment of the akam heroine, so giving it up shows how completely her life is ordered around him. The umm in kannum ('even the eyes') implies she forgoes other adornment too. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree on 'lest he be hidden'; Pope: 'My love doth ever in my eyes reside; / I stain them not, fearing his form to hide.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa's Cloud Messenger, the exiled yaksha imagines his wife at home giving up her ornaments, her hair bound in a single plain braid, as she waits for him.
hinduism.explanation: In Sanskrit poetry, a devoted woman lays aside adornment while her beloved is absent, because there is no one she wishes to adorn herself for.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also gives up adornment for her lover's sake, though for the playful reason that he lives in her eyes.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; the forgoing of adornment for love matches, but the motive is separation-grief rather than the Kural's conceit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart”
christianity.explanation: Peter advises that true beauty is the inner person, not outward adornment.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's heroine sets aside outward adornment for the sake of the one she carries within, a 'hidden man' of her own.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); it shares the setting-aside of adornment for something inward, but the motive is moral, not romantic.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an directs believing women not to display their adornment except to their husbands and close family.
islam.explanation: Adornment is treated as something that belongs within the bond of marriage.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's heroine arranges her adornment entirely around her beloved; Islam likewise orients a wife's adornment toward her husband.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified word for word this session; a next-best match on adornment directed to the beloved, in a context of modesty law.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jeremiah warns faithless Judah that though she paints her eyes and puts on finery to attract lovers, she beautifies herself in vain.
judaism.explanation: The prophet uses eye-paint as the image of adornment that seeks the wrong love.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine refuses eye-paint out of faithfulness to her one lover, the reverse of the prophet's image of faithless adornment.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified word for word this session; a next-best match built on eye-paint, used as a negative image.

buddhism.quote_or_event: On the Uposatha observance days, lay followers take extra precepts, including abstaining from garlands, perfumes and cosmetics.
buddhism.explanation: Setting aside adornment is a Buddhist practice of restraint, done for one's own spiritual progress.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also lays aside cosmetics, but out of love for the one in her eyes rather than for restraint.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a next-best match on giving up cosmetics, for a different reason.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra lists the use of collyrium on the eyes among the practices forbidden to a Jain monk.
jainism.explanation: Even eye-cosmetics count as self-adornment that feeds attachment to the body.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine gives up kohl out of love; the Jain monk gives it up out of detachment.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; it shares the specific detail of forgoing collyrium but for opposite reasons.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When her maid urges Penelope to wash and anoint her face before appearing to the suitors, she refuses, saying the gods destroyed her beauty on the day Odysseus sailed for Troy.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope's refusal to beautify herself is a sign of loyalty to her absent husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's heroine, Penelope lays aside adornment for the one she loves.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a strong fit on forgoing adornment out of love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Socrates calls cosmetics a flattering imitation of gymnastics, giving a false appearance of beauty instead of real health.
philosophy.explanation: Plato distrusts adornment as a counterfeit of genuine good.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also sets cosmetics aside, though from love, not from Plato's suspicion of appearances.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a weak next-best match that shares only the rejection of cosmetics.

kurals.tamil:
நெஞ்சத்தார் காத லவராக வெய்துண்டல்
அஞ்சுதும் வேபாக் கறிந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Nenjaththaar kaadha lavaraaga veydhundal
anjudhum vaepaak karindhu.
kurals.meaning: Because my lover lives in my heart, I am afraid to eat anything hot, knowing it would burn him.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever carried a baby bird very carefully so it wouldn't get hurt? The girl in this poem feels her love is living right inside her chest, so she won't even drink something hot in case it burns him.
kurals.university: The conceit moves from the eyes to the heart: nenjaththaar (நெஞ்சத்தார், 'he who is in my heart') is so literally present that veydhu undal (வெய்துண்டல், eating hot food) is feared (anjudhum, அஞ்சுதும்) because of vaepaakku (வேபாக்கு, his being scorched). The first person plural is the heroine's dignified 'we'. All four commentators on thirukkural.net and ytamizh.com agree on the sense; Kalaignar generalises it into a definition: true lovers are those so blended heart with heart that they fear hot food might burn the other. Pope: 'Within my heart my lover dwells; from food I turn / That smacks of heat, lest he should feel it burn.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O dearly beloved! Your lotus feet are so soft that we place them gently on our breasts, fearing that Your feet will be hurt.”
hinduism.explanation: In their song of separation the gopis tell Krishna they fear even their own bodies might hurt his tender feet, and worry about him on the stony forest paths.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly as the Kural's heroine fears her own hot food might burn the lover within her, the gopis fear their own bodies might hurt their beloved.
hinduism.source: Srimad Bhagavatam 10.31.19 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, vedabase.io)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a near one-to-one match of a lover's fear that her own body might hurt the beloved.

christianity.quote_or_event: “That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love,”
christianity.explanation: Paul prays that Christ will make his home in the believers' hearts.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's beloved also lives in the heroine's heart; Paul uses the same image of a dear one dwelling within.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good fit on the beloved dwelling in the heart, without the protective conceit.

islam.quote_or_event: “We are closer to him than [his] jugular vein”
islam.explanation: God declares that He is nearer to a person than the vein in his own neck.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's beloved is so near he is inside the heart; the Qur'an expresses a closeness even nearer than the body's own veins.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; matches the intimacy of presence inside the body, in a theological rather than romantic sense.

judaism.quote_or_event: The bride of the Song of Songs asks her beloved to set her as a seal upon his heart and upon his arm, for love is strong as death.
judaism.explanation: The seal on the heart is the image of a beloved permanently imprinted within.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine likewise carries her beloved inside her heart and guards him there.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified word for word this session; a strong fit on the beloved held in the heart, without the burning conceit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even as a mother protects with her life / Her child, her only child, / So with a boundless heart / Should one cherish all living beings”
buddhism.explanation: The Metta Sutta takes a mother's protective love as the model for boundless kindness.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine guards the beloved within her as anxiously as a mother guards her only child.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 1.8, Karaniya Metta Sutta (tr. The Amaravati Sangha)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight; matches protective tenderness, but directed to all beings rather than one beloved.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga Sutra teaches that fire-bodies, water-bodies and other tiny, unseen beings are alive, and that a careful person avoids harming them even in ordinary acts like cooking and eating.
jainism.explanation: Jain ahimsa extends care to beings too small to be seen, shaping how one eats and drinks.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine changes how she eats to avoid harming an unseen beloved; Jain practice changes how one eats to avoid harming unseen life.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.1 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a structural parallel of careful eating for an invisible being's sake, without romance.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Psyche secretly lights a lamp to look at her sleeping husband Cupid, a drop of hot oil falls on his shoulder and burns him, and he flies away.
greek_mythology.explanation: Psyche's moment of curiosity hurts the beloved she had never seen and costs her his presence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's heroine fears exactly this: that something hot from her might burn the lover she carries.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known tale (preserved in Latin by Apuleius); a vivid parallel of a lover accidentally burning the beloved.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for he walks not upon the earth, nor yet upon skulls of men, which are not so very soft, but in the hearts and souls of both god, and men, which are of all things the softest: in them he walks and dwells and makes his home.”
philosophy.explanation: In Plato's Symposium, Agathon praises Love as the tenderest of gods, who lives only in soft and gentle hearts.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover also makes his home in the heart, and the heroine guards that tender place from anything that could burn him.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 195e, speech of Agathon (tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (including its printing 'god,'); a strong fit on Love dwelling in tender hearts.

kurals.tamil:
இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல் அனைத்திற்கே
ஏதிலர் என்னும்இவ் வூர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Imaippin karappaakku arival anaiththirkae
aedhilar ennumiv voor.
kurals.meaning: I know that if I blink he will be hidden, so I keep my eyes open; and for that alone this town calls him unloving.
kurals.elementary: Suppose you stayed up late because you were thinking about someone you love, and the next day people said, 'That person must be unkind to keep you awake!' The girl in this poem says the town blames her lover, though really it is just her love that keeps her eyes open.
kurals.university: The heroine explains her sleeplessness: she will not close her eyes because she knows that on blinking (imaippin) he would be hidden (karappaakku). Seeing her wakeful and pale, the ur (ஊர், 'town') concludes that he is aedhilar (ஏதிலர், 'a stranger, one without love') who has abandoned her, and she protests the injustice. Anaiththirkae ('for just that much') marks the town's verdict as unfair. This introduces alar (அலர், gossip), the theme of ch. 115. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pulavar Kesikan agree; Kalaignar adds that the town blames him for the 'pain of sleeplessness'. Pope: 'I fear his form to hide, nor close my eyes: / "Her love estranged is gone!" the village cries.' The second line is shared verbatim with 1130, a deliberate refrain. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “even when we can eagerly look upon Your beautiful face, so lovely with its adornment of curly locks, our pleasure is hindered by our eyelids, which were fashioned by the foolish creator.”
hinduism.explanation: The gopis complain to Krishna that even blinking costs them a glimpse of him, and blame the creator for making eyelids at all.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also refuses to blink for fear of losing sight of her lover; the gopis wish their eyelids had never been made.
hinduism.source: Srimad Bhagavatam 10.31.15 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, vedabase.io)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io (italics dropped from 'can'); a near one-to-one match of the blinking motif.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh”
christianity.explanation: The woman in the Song of Songs lies down to rest but her heart stays awake, alert for her beloved.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's heroine likewise stays awake for her lover, even if in her case it is her eyes that will not close.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good fit on wakefulness for the beloved, without the town's gossip.

islam.quote_or_event: “My eyes sleep, but my heart does not sleep.”
islam.explanation: Asked whether he sleeps before the night prayer, the Prophet answers that only his eyes rest while his heart stays awake.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's heroine keeps her eyes open for the sake of the one in her heart; the Prophet's heart stays awake while his eyes sleep.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a next-best match on sleep and wakefulness, in a devotional rather than romantic context.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I will not give sleep to mine eyes, Nor slumber to mine eyelids;”
judaism.explanation: The psalm recalls David's vow not to rest until he had found a dwelling place for God.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also refuses to let her eyelids close for the sake of the one she loves.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; closely matches the eyelid image, though the vow is about devotion to God.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are ever vigilant, who discipline themselves day and night, and are ever intent upon Nibbana — their defilements fade away.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises wakefulness and vigilance, day and night, as the path to liberation.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine is wakeful for love; Buddhism prizes the same unsleeping vigilance for the opposite goal of freedom from attachment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight; a next-best match on wakefulness with a different purpose.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The Venerable One, exerting himself, did not seek sleep for the sake of pleasure; he waked up himself, and slept only a little, free from desires.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga describes Mahavira staying almost sleepless during his years of austerity, out of vigilance rather than desire.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also barely sleeps, but out of love; Mahavira's wakefulness is the ascetic counterpart.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.8.2.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a match on deliberate sleeplessness, with the opposite motive.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hera sets the hundred-eyed Argus to guard Io; he never closes all his eyes at once, so that some are always watching.
greek_mythology.explanation: Argus is the Greek image of a watcher who never fully sleeps.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's heroine also refuses to close her eyes, though she watches for love, not on a goddess's orders.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth; a weak next-best match that shares only the never-closing eyes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal observes that the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: For Pascal, love follows a logic that outsiders reasoning coolly cannot see.
philosophy.tie_back: The town judges the heroine's sleeplessness by outward signs and blames her lover; it cannot see the heart's real reason.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous line, not verified against a published translation this session; a good fit on outsiders misreading love.

kurals.tamil:
உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும் இகந்துறைவர்
ஏதிலர் என்னும்இவ் வூர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uvandhuraivar ullaththul endrum igandhuraivar
aedhilar ennumiv voor.
kurals.meaning: He lives happily in my heart always, yet this town says he lives far away and does not love me.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes people only see what is on the outside. Someone might think two friends have drifted apart because they live in different places, but the friends know they still care about each other every day. The girl in this poem says her love is always in her heart, even if the town thinks he is gone.
kurals.university: The chapter closes by contrasting uvandhu uraivar (உவந்துறைவர், 'he dwells rejoicing') ullaththul endrum ('in my heart always') with the town's verdict that he igandhu uraivar (இகந்துறைவர், 'lives having gone away') and is aedhilar, unloving. The repetition of uraivar and the refrain line shared with 1129 sharpen the irony: physical distance is visible to the town, but inner presence is visible only to her. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pulavar Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree; Pope: 'Rejoicing in my very soul he ever lies; / "Her love estranged is gone far off!" the village cries.' Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You are never actually separated from Me, for I am the Soul of all creation.”
hinduism.explanation: Through his messenger Uddhava, Krishna tells the grieving gopis of Vraja that although he has gone to Mathura he is never truly apart from them.
hinduism.tie_back: Just as the Kural's heroine insists that her absent lover still dwells within her, Krishna assures the gopis that he dwells within them though others see only his absence.
hinduism.source: Srimad Bhagavatam 10.47.29 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, vedabase.io)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a close match on inner presence despite outward separation, framed theologically.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns his critics not to judge by what things look like on the surface.
christianity.tie_back: The town in the Kural judges the absent lover by appearances; the heroine knows the truth within.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good fit on misjudging by appearances, without the love theme.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an forbids jumping to suspicious conclusions about others and backbiting.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's town assumes the worst of an absent lover; the Qur'an names such assumption a sin.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; a good fit on condemning suspicious gossip.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Samuel is impressed by the appearance of Jesse's eldest son, God tells him that people look on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.
judaism.explanation: The story teaches that the truth of a person lies in the heart, not in what is outwardly visible.
judaism.tie_back: The town sees only the lover's absence; the heroine, like God in the story, sees what is in the heart.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified word for word this session; a good fit on judging by appearance versus the heart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “O Atula! Indeed, this is an ancient practice, not one only of today: they blame those who remain silent, they blame those who speak much, they blame those who speak in moderation. There is none in the world who is not blamed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada observes that people will find fault with anyone, whatever they do.
buddhism.tie_back: The town finds fault with the heroine's lover no matter what; the Buddha says such blame is as old as the world.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight; a good fit on unfair public blame.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the resting-places there once, in a night, the single wanderers asked him (who he was, and why he was there); as he did not answer, they treated him badly; but he persevered in his meditations, free from resentment.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga records how people who did not understand Mahavira's silent practice misjudged and mistreated him.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's town also misreads what it cannot see, judging the lover by outward signs.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.8.2.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares only the theme of outsiders misjudging what they do not understand.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After her husband Protesilaus dies at Troy, Laodamia keeps a likeness of him in her room; a servant who sees her embracing it assumes she has a secret lover and reports her to her father.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her family misreads her devotion to her absent husband as betrayal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's town, onlookers misjudge a love they cannot see from outside.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a close fit on outsiders misreading devotion to an absent beloved.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the allegory of the cave, prisoners who see only shadows on a wall take them for the whole of reality.
philosophy.explanation: Plato's image shows how people who see only surfaces mistake them for the truth.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's town sees only the lover's absence and takes it for lack of love, while the heroine knows the reality within.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very well-known passage; a next-best match on appearance versus reality, without the love theme.
